title: Improving Regulatory Transparency for New Medical Therapies Act
official_summary:
(This measure has not been amended since it was passed by the Senate on October 26, 2015. The summary of that version is repeated here.)

Improving Regulatory Transparency for New Medical Therapies Act

(Sec. 2) This bill amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and the Public Health Service Act to delay the effective date of approval of a drug, biological product, or animal drug for which the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recommends controls under the Controlled Substances Act until the Department of Justice (DOJ) issues a final interim rule for the drug. This delay also applies to conditional approval and indexing of animal drugs.

This bill amends the Controlled Substances Act to require the DOJ to issue a final interim rule for a drug product recommended for controls by the FDA not later than 90 days after DOJ receives a recommendation for controls or the FDA approves the drug. The final interim rule is effective immediately.

For purposes of submitting an application to extend a patent, a drug product recommended for controls is considered to be approved and have permission for commercial marketing and use on the date of FDA approval or the date an interim final rule is issued, whichever is later.

(Sec. 3) Timelines are established for DOJ to either register an applicant to manufacture a controlled substance for a clinical trial or serve an order to show cause upon the applicant.

(Sec. 4) This bill amends the Controlled Substances Import and Export Act to allow exported controlled substances to be re-exported within the European Economic Area.

summary.headline: This law sets deadlines for the Justice Department to set controls on new drugs that the FDA says could be abused, and changes rules on approvals, patent extensions, clinical trial registration, and exports.
summary.what_it_does: The law delays FDA approval of certain drugs, biological products, and animal drugs that the FDA recommends placing under the Controlled Substances Act until the Justice Department issues a final interim rule for them. The Justice Department must issue that rule within 90 days after it gets the FDA's recommendation or the FDA approves the drug, and the rule takes effect immediately. The law also treats these drugs as approved for patent-extension purposes on the later of the FDA approval date or the interim rule date, and it sets timelines for the Justice Department to register clinical trial manufacturers or issue an order to show cause. Finally, it lets controlled substances that were exported be re-exported within the European Economic Area.

who_it_affects.group: Drug and biological product manufacturers seeking FDA approval for drugs the FDA may recommend for controls
who_it_affects.how: Their FDA approval can be delayed until the Justice Department finishes its interim rule, which must come within 90 days.
Approval, conditional approval, and indexing of their drugs can be delayed under the same process when controls are recommended.

who_it_affects.group: Companies seeking patent extensions for controlled-substance drugs
who_it_affects.how: The date used for their patent-extension applications is the later of FDA approval or the interim rule date.

who_it_affects.group: Applicants to manufacture controlled substances for clinical trials
who_it_affects.how: The Justice Department must either register them or serve an order to show cause within set timelines.

who_it_affects.group: Companies that export controlled substances to Europe
who_it_affects.how: They may re-export those substances within the European Economic Area under the amended import and export law.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: Signed into law on November 25, 2015; the summary does not list separate effective dates for each section.
